intro_en:
This segment of the Israel National Trail, together with the segment south of it, crosses the Avdat plateau from the Zin Valley to Makhtesh Ramon. In the present segment we scale the Tzinim Cliff to Hod Akev, a prominent peak above the Zin Valley. We pass the springs that emerge at the foot of the cliff, Ein Akev and Ein Shaviv, and walk along the eastern edge of the Avdat plateau above the Zin Valley.

 Nahal Ofran – Hod Akev (40)
 Nahal Hava – Mitzpe Ramon (42)
character_en: Ascents and descents, some of them steep and demanding effort
pois_en: Hod Akev, Ein Akev, Upper Ein Akev, Ein Shaviv, the Oil Road
important_en: Access to the starting point at the foot of Hod Akev, and to the end point at the Nahal Hava overnight campsite, is possible by 4x4 vehicle only.
The ascent of Hod Akev from the north is steep, and may be challenging for those who struggle with a fear of heights.
The nature reserve in the Zin Valley is highly sensitive.
After dark, the entire reserve area belongs to the animals, the reserve's permanent residents. Do not wander outside the designated overnight campsites.
description_en:
We set out from the overnight campsite at the foot of Hod Akev along a red-marked trail, to climb the Tzinim Cliff to Hod Akev. Those who slept at Midreshet Sde Boker return to the Israel National Trail with a walk of about 5 km, partly downhill.
The Tzinim Cliff is the northern and eastern edge of the Avdat plateau, towards the Zin Valley. The Avdat plateau, unlike the anticlines and ridges in the makhtesh region, is built of horizontal layers of young rock (Eocene age). This is pale, soft rock, chalk and limestone, with flint nodules and lenses embedded in it.
The Tzinim Cliff was formed as a result of rapid weathering processes as Nahal Zin cut down towards the Dead Sea rift. The top of the cliff stands about 200 metres above the Zin Valley. To understand why this is one of the more challenging climbs on the Israel National Trail, note that the start at the overnight campsite is at 330 metres above sea level, the top of the cliff that we pass over during the climb is at 500 metres, and Hod Akev stands at about 570 metres.
The trail climbs a white spur, a kind of ramp that covers the lower step of the cliff and allows us to climb to the foot of its upper step. The trail continues below the upper step to a point where the step is lower. At this point there are handholds and an iron ladder that help with the climb to the top of the cliff, bringing us onto the plateau.
The dome of Hod Akev looks close; a white trail climbs to its summit and another trail skirts around it. We climb to the summit along the green-marked trail.
From the "Hod" (the point) there is a fine 360-degree view. To the north is the Hatira Ridge, the ridge of the Large Makhtesh (HaMakhtesh HaGadol), and between Hod Akev and the Hatira Ridge lie the Zin Valley and Nahal Zin.
On the plateau to the north-west are two green patches: Kibbutz Sde Boker on the right and the Midrasha on the left. At the foot of the Midrasha winds Nahal Zin, and from the south Nahal Akev joins it. The stream channels can be identified by their vegetation, whose green colour contrasts with the pale colour around them.
We descend from Hod Akev with the trail towards Ein Akev. At the meeting with the main channel of Nahal Akev, the trail colour changes to blue. After a short walk up the stream, we reach Ein Akev.
Ein Akev forms a beautiful pool at the foot of a waterfall. It is one of several springs that emerge in the stream channels cut into this part of the Avdat plateau. The water is brackish and the flow is low, but here in the desert it is a permanent and important source of water for sustaining the natural wildlife and plant life. In the channel there is water vegetation: reeds, tamarisk, rushes and other species. The springs serve as a water source for animals: molluscs, birds and mammals, the most prominent of which is the ibex. The animals come to drink mainly in the early morning hours and at dusk, so it is important to leave the area of the springs at those hours to avoid disturbing the animals.
We return with a short walk along the channel, on the left bank and past a group of palm trees. We climb with the blue trail, going up the step in the channel wall with the help of handholds.
The trail passes above the Ein Akev waterfall and continues up the stream southward towards Upper Ein Akev, another spring in Nahal Akev. For a short stretch, green marking accompanies the trail, after which the marking colour changes to black.
Approaching the spring of Upper Ein Akev, reeds appear in the stream channel, followed by flowing water as well, the waters of Upper Ein Akev. The trail crosses to the right bank through the reeds and reaches a trail junction. The blue trail connects the ancient city of Avdat with Ein Shaviv. Avdat was a Nabataean city on the trade route of the Incense Route, which connected Petra with the port of Gaza.
The Israel National Trail continues up Nahal Akev with the blue trail. A short distance after the water vegetation accompanying the springs ends, the trail curves within the channel eastward and climbs to the plateau above.
We walk some distance along the plateau until a fine view opens up towards the Zin Valley. The trail runs along the edge of the plateau, while in the channel below a green patch of vegetation around Ein Zik can be seen.
A short distance later the steep descent to Ein Shaviv begins, another spring that emerges at the foot of the Tzinim Cliff. Ein Shaviv is crowned with a grove of Euphrates poplars, a wild tree that grows beside water. The poplar puts on a beautiful autumn display as its leaves turn yellow. The tree bears leaves of two shapes: elongated and rectangular. Its reproduction also takes two forms: local propagation by sending up shoots from the roots (vegetative reproduction), and reproduction that allows long-distance dispersal by means of small seeds wrapped in long silky hairs that help the seeds spread with the wind (sexual reproduction). This mechanism allows the seeds to reach new moist habitats, even distant and isolated ones.
The trail crosses the grove of poplars and palms in the channel of Nahal Zik, a true desert oasis, and returns to the desert and the Tzinim Cliff, with another climb back up to the plateau. The ascent is steep at first, overcomes the step of the cliff and then becomes more moderate.
On the back of the plateau, the trail meets a dirt track known as the "Oil Road". From here the track and the trail head south along the route of the Eilat-Ashkelon oil pipeline. The pipeline created a land bridge between the Gulf of Eilat and the Mediterranean coast, parallel to the sea route through the Suez Canal. Iranian oil flowed through the line until the Islamic Revolution in 1979. After the signing of the peace treaty with Egypt, Egyptian fuel from Sinai passed through the line until 1994. Today fuel flows in both directions through the old pipeline (you are invited to read here about the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel's struggle against the environmental dangers of the oil pipeline).
The track continues in an almost straight line towards the south-east and is marked black. After about 2 km we reach a trail junction; the black trail turns left onto a footpath that descends Ma'ale "Nahash Tzame" (Thirsty Snake Ascent), and the Israel National Trail continues along a track with green marking.
At this point the trail is close to the Tzinim Cliff, and from here there is a fine view towards the Zin Valley. Beyond the valley are the Hatira Ridge, the Hatzera Ridge and Har Zin (Hor HaHar). Ma'ale Nahash Tzame descends to the Zin Valley and passes near the Tzinim excavations, a failed project that included two tunnels drilled beside the oil pipeline to serve as large oil storage tanks; entering the excavations is considered dangerous.
We continue south along the Oil Road; the trail defies the topography, "stitching" across spurs and channels, and reaches a trail junction at the top of one of the spurs. A red trail leaves the junction eastward to Horvat Sharav, and a black-marked track reaches the junction from the west, from Road 40. Beside the junction is the end point of the segment at the Nahal Hava overnight campsite.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, trail marking coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel
